% =====================================================================
\section*{Abstract}
% =====================================================================

Linguistic dating assumes that a late author cannot convincingly write like an
early one, and that the language of a text carries its date rather than its
subject.  Both are tested here on \HBwords{} words of anchored Biblical Hebrew,
partitioned into \HBchunks{} passages of about \HBtarget{} words.  Genre, not chronology, proves to be the dominant axis
of variation: \GNbetween\% of the variance in the model's predictions lies
between genres, and rank correlation with true date falls from $\GNrhoRaw$ to
$\GNrhoPartial$ once genre is held fixed.  A permutation null shuffling dates
only within genre confirms that a chronological signal survives ($p =
\GNnullP$), but the surviving signal is entirely lexical---refitting on
morphosyntax alone gives $\RTBgenre$---and includes the classical-to-late
first-person pronoun shift, recovered unsupervised in the correct direction.
Across \SPpass{} analytic specifications the Deuteronomic and Priestly sources
fall after the exile in every one and the JE composite in \SPJEpost, in the
classical order JE $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ P, with central estimates in
the Persian period and intervals too wide to quote any single date.  Within the sources, D is measurably the most homogeneous; but the apparent
separations between each source's conventional blocks are significant on the
full feature set and dissolve under the genre control, the Deuteronomic one
reversing.  They are register effects, not dates.  Archaizing was tested separately, with opposite outcomes in
the two languages.  Substituting the recognized Classical forms throughout six
securely dated late Hebrew books moves their estimates by \arcMeanAbs{} years,
which is \DETpct\% of this model's residual scale: a non-detection, not a
measurement that archaizing is cheap.  In Greek, where the archaizing
is real and its practitioners known, the Second Sophistic Atticizers are placed
\GKattshiftAbs{} years too early---\GKwithinAbs{} against texts of their own
genre---by a model trained on non-archaizing Greek.  Deliberate imitation can displace a
linguistic date by centuries, and the poems dated here should be read with that
possibility open.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Introduction}
% =====================================================================

Scholars in biblical studies, classical philology, and Near Eastern
linguistics routinely use internal linguistic evidence to constrain the dates
of ancient texts.  The transition from Classical Biblical Hebrew (\cbh{}; also
called Standard Biblical Hebrew) to Late Biblical Hebrew (\lbh{}) is among the
best-documented diachronic shifts in any ancient
language~\cite{Hurvitz1982,Rooker1990,Polzin1976}, and comparable transitions
are well attested in Ancient Greek~\cite{Horrocks2010} and Akkadian.  The
practice has an obvious appeal for the Pentateuch, whose sources carry no
colophons and whose dates have been argued from literary and historical
grounds for two centuries.

I set out to produce calibrated dates for those sources.  The main finding of
this article is that the linguistic evidence supports much less than the
literature assumes, and that the largest obstacle is not the one the field has
been arguing about.

That obstacle is genre.  In a corpus assembled by date, genre rather than
chronology turns out to be the dominant axis of variation: \GNbetween\% of the
variance in the model's predictions lies between genres, and rank correlation
with true date falls from $\GNrhoRaw$ to $\GNrhoPartial$ once genre is held
fixed.  A permutation null that shuffles dates only within genre---preserving
the genre--date association the corpus happens to contain and destroying only
the within-genre chronology---confirms that a chronological signal survives ($p
= \GNnullP$).  But it is roughly half the raw figure, and studies in this
literature that report raw correlations without a genre control are overstating
their evidence.  The surviving signal is moreover entirely lexical: refitting on
verb morphology, clause structure and agreement, with every lexeme removed,
gives $\RTBgenre$.  Whatever grammatical change occurred over this period is
not detectable at this sample size.

What the evidence does support is a placement claim.  Across \SPpass{}
defensible analytic specifications the Deuteronomic and Priestly sources fall
after the exile without exception, and the JE composite in \SPJEpost{} of them,
in the classical sequence JE $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ P, with central
estimates in the Persian period.  The intervals are roughly \SPPhalf~yr wide at
68\% on either side, and no individual date in this study should be quoted to a
century.  I report the full specification curve rather than a preferred
configuration, because no configuration here has a strong claim to being the
right one.

Within the sources the picture is mixed, and the negative half of it is worth as
much as the positive.  The Deuteronomic source is measurably the most internally
homogeneous of the three, and that holds however hard the genre-diagnostic
features are screened out.  But the separations between each source's
conventional blocks---the Deuteronomic law code from its narrative frame, the
Holiness Code from the Priestly material of Leviticus 1--16, the JE material of
Genesis from that of Exodus---behave differently.  On the full feature set all
three are significant and all three point the way the critical literature would
predict.  Under the genre control they vanish, and the Deuteronomic separation
reverses and becomes significant in the opposite direction.  The law code is
legal prose and its frame is hortatory narrative; the gap between them was
carried by the vocabulary that distinguishes those registers.  I report this at
length because the unscreened numbers are exactly what a study would publish if
it stopped one step early, and because it shows what the genre control is for.

Beneath the whole enterprise sits an assumption that is stated often and tested
never.  Linguistic dating presupposes that a late author cannot convincingly
write like an early one.  Were deliberate archaizing easy, so that a
Persian-period scribe could adopt Classical vocabulary and thereby acquire a
Classical date, every linguistic argument for the antiquity of a biblical text
would be worthless, and the objection would apply to traditional and
computational methods alike.  The dialectal school has pressed this point for
two decades~\cite{Young2008,Rezetko2014}, while the mainstream reply has been
that sustained archaizing is difficult.  Both positions are assertions.
Neither side has put a number on the matter.

Archaizing is therefore tested here twice, and the two tests do not come out
the same way.  I can perform archaizing myself, so the ground truth is known
exactly: securely dated \emph{late} books have their \lbh{} forms replaced by
\cbh{} counterparts at controlled rates, every feature is re-extracted from the
altered text, and the result is dated by a model that never saw it.  The
displacement this produces is far below the model's own noise, so what the
Hebrew experiment establishes is that archaizing of that kind cannot be detected
here---not that it would be cheap for a scribe.
Ancient Greek then supplies what Hebrew cannot, namely texts whose authors
really did archaize, deliberately and expertly, and whose dates of composition
are securely known.  The Second Sophistic Atticizers wrote imitation Classical
Attic four to seven centuries after the fact, taught by a formal curriculum,
well enough to be read as models of style for a millennium.  This prices the
\emph{morphosyntactic} mechanism, and the price is an order of magnitude
higher.  The Greek measurement is put through the same genre control as the
Hebrew one, and survives it: Atticizing texts are dated \GKwithinAbs~yr
earlier than non-archaizing texts of the same genre.

That contrast is what this study offers against the standing objection, and it
is narrower than a price list.  Where archaizing is real and documented it
displaces a linguistic date by centuries, which settles that the objection has
teeth.  Where it is simulated by substituting diagnostic vocabulary, this model
cannot see it at all, which settles only that this model is the wrong instrument
for that question.  Whether a given text could have been archaized therefore
turns on what its author was trained to do---a historical question about scribal
education, not a statistical one---and on an instrument more sensitive than this
one.

The Background section reviews the CBH/LBH distinction, the dialectal
challenge, and the problem of circularity.  The Data section describes the
anchored corpus, the passage-level design, and feature extraction.  The Model
section presents the weighted ridge estimator, the variance-matching step, and
the jackknife+ intervals.  The Validation section documents a failure mode that
inflates reported accuracy in this literature, establishes the genre confound
and the lexical character of the signal, and reports leave-one-book-out
performance against two permutation nulls.  The two Results sections report the
internal structure of the sources and their placement relative to the exile,
and the section following them reports both archaizing measurements.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Background: Diachronic Biblical Hebrew}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{The CBH/LBH Distinction}

Classical Biblical Hebrew (\cbh{}) is the language of the pre-exilic prophetic
corpus and early narrative material (8th--7th centuries BCE): Amos, Hosea,
early Isaiah, and the narrative strands of Samuel--Kings.  Late Biblical
Hebrew (\lbh{}) characterizes the post-exilic prose of Ezra, Nehemiah,
Chronicles, Esther, and Daniel (5th--2nd centuries BCE).

The transition is marked by well-studied lexical, morphological, and syntactic
changes~\cite{Hurvitz1997,Rooker1990,Polzin1976,Young2003}.  At the lexical
level, the first-person singular pronoun shifts from \textit{ank\={\i}} to
\textit{an\={\i}}; the relative pronoun \textit{ašer} gives way to the enclitic
\textit{š}e-; the negator \textit{l\={o}\textquotesingle} is supplemented by
and partly replaced by \textit{\textquotesingle \={e}n}.  At the morphological
level, the wayyiqtol declines in frequency while the \textit{h\={a}y\={a}h} +
participle periphrastic increases.  At the syntactic level,
infinitive-absolute constructions rise, and sentence structure shifts toward
analytic patterns associated with Aramaic
influence~\cite{Young2008,Rezetko2014}.

The consensus
view~\cite{Hurvitz1982,Hurvitz2014,Robertson1972,Schniedewind2004} holds that
these features shift monotonically along the temporal axis, constituting a
reliable if noisy diachronic signal.  The present study adopts this view as a
working assumption and then tests the principal alternative to it directly.

\subsection*{Diachronic or Dialectal}

Young, Rezetko, and Ehrensv\"{a}rd~\cite{Young2008} argue that the CBH/LBH
contrast may reflect geographic dialect, scribal tradition, or literary
register rather than chronology.  The Qumran sectarian texts
($\sim$150~BCE) deliberately employ \cbh{} vocabulary and morphology while
simultaneously using Aramaic loan-words --- a pattern they interpret as
literary register rather than temporal reality.  Hurvitz and the diachronic
mainstream~\cite{Hurvitz1997} counter that the dialectal alternatives require
additional auxiliary hypotheses, and that the Qumran archaism case
presupposes the original \cbh{} features had already receded, confirming
rather than undermining the diachronic interpretation.

This debate has been conducted almost entirely through argument.  Its empirical
core, however, is a quantitative question: how much apparent antiquity does
deliberate archaizing actually purchase?  That question is answerable.  A model
that assigns dates can be fed texts whose archaizing status is known, either
because I performed the archaizing myself or because the author's
imitative program is a matter of literary-historical record.  Both experiments
are reported below.  Neither resolves the dispute, but each supplies a
measurement that either side can now argue from, which is more than the debate
has had so far.

\subsection*{The Problem of Circularity}

Dating methods that use features identified by comparing texts of assumed date
risk circularity: the assumed dates shape the feature set, and the feature set
is then used to infer unknown dates.  Three safeguards are adopted.

A distinction is necessary before the safeguards can be stated, because the
objection applies with very different force to different kinds of evidence.
Dating a text by its resemblance to other Hebrew of supposed date is circular
for the present purpose, since it invokes the very cline the model is meant to
estimate.  Dating a text by a datable referent is not.  Esther's Achaemenid
court and administration, the fall of Nineveh behind Nahum, and the Persian
administrative vocabulary of Ecclesiastes are all anchored to events and
language contacts documented outside the biblical tradition.  That Esther cannot
be pre-exilic follows from Persian history, not from Hebrew style, and the
inference would stand were the language of Esther entirely unremarkable.  The
same logic underwrites Ezekiel's regnal dates.  They are evidence because the
kings and years can be checked against Babylonian records; had he invented them,
they would be worth nothing.

The circularity that has damaged linguistic dating runs in the other direction,
and it runs through the Torah.  The pre-exilic standard against which lateness
is measured was itself constructed in part from Torah texts assumed to be
pre-exilic, and those texts were then dated by their conformity to
it~\cite{Young2008,Rezetko2014}.  Nothing in the present design enters that
loop.  The model learns the feature-to-date mapping from the anchored corpus
alone, no Torah text is used in training, and every Torah estimate is therefore
a genuine out-of-sample prediction.

With that distinction in place, three safeguards apply.

First, every training date rests on a synchronism or on a datable historical
referent.  Twelve of the \HBbooks{} units carry an explicit synchronism, a named
ruler or regnal year checkable against Assyrian, Babylonian, or Persian records;
twelve more are fixed by a datable event, institution, or language contact.
One unit, Jonah, is dated principally on typological grounds, and its removal is
reported in Table~\ref{tab:anchors}.

Second, no feature is selected using date information.  The feature set is
fixed in advance by frequency rank in the corpus as a whole (Data section),
not by correlation with date.  Feature-by-date screening was evaluated and
rejected: at this dimensionality the false discovery proportion among
screened features is high enough that screening manufactures apparent signal
(S2 Table).

Third, all reported performance comes from leave-one-\emph{book}-out
cross-validation in which standardization, weighting, regularization-parameter
selection and interval calibration are performed inside each fold, and
significance is established by a permutation null that re-runs the entire
pipeline on shuffled dates.

\textbf{Why an anchored corpus.}  The Hebrew prophetic books offer a form of
historical anchoring available nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible: their
superscriptions and internal chronological notices can be cross-checked
against records entirely external to the biblical tradition.  Ezekiel
explicitly dates thirteen of his visions to regnal years of the Babylonian
exile --- ``the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity'' (Ezek~1:2), ``the
sixth year'' (8:1), and so forth --- which correlate with Babylonian
administrative texts independently dating Jehoiachin's deportation to
597~BCE.  Other eighth- and seventh-century prophets (Amos, Hosea, Isaiah,
Micah, Zephaniah, Nahum) are anchored by superscriptions naming Judahite and
Israelite kings whose reigns are documented in the Assyrian and
Neo-Babylonian annals.  No comparable external anchoring exists for the Torah
or the poetic books: their dates derive entirely from literary-critical
argument, which is precisely the circularity this study seeks to avoid.

\textbf{Asymmetric error and conservative upper bounds on antiquity.}  If the
accepted dates for the anchored training texts were wrong, the error would be
asymmetric: these texts can be \emph{no older} than the historical events they
reference, but they could in principle be \emph{younger}.  A training corpus
misdated in the direction of being too early would calibrate the
feature-to-date mapping at too early a point on the temporal axis, so unknown
texts dated against that calibration would also be estimated as too early.
Any systematic error in the training dates therefore propagates in a single
direction: all model-derived dates shift toward greater recency.  The dates
reported here should be read as \emph{conservative upper bounds on
antiquity}.  A text dated to 400~BCE may be more recent; the linguistic
evidence provides no support for a date earlier than the estimate.

\subsection*{Prior Computational Work: Attribution versus Dating}

Computational approaches to textual attribution and stylometric dating have a
substantial history, from Mosteller and Wallace's Bayesian analysis of the
Federalist Papers~\cite{Mosteller1984} through the stylometric tradition
surveyed by Holmes~\cite{Holmes1998} and the function-word methods of
Burrows~\cite{Burrows2002}.  Among work applied specifically to the Hebrew
Bible, Faigenbaum-Golovin et al.~\cite{Faigenbaum2025} provide the most
methodologically rigorous prior computational treatment.  Their Higher
Criticism discrepancy method tests whether the distribution of lemma n-gram
frequencies in a target text deviates from the null that it was produced by
the same process as a reference corpus.  Applied to 50 ground-truth chapters
spanning D, the Deuteronomistic History, and P, it achieves 84\% attribution
accuracy in leave-one-out validation and yields interpretable discriminating
lemma lists.

The present framework answers a different question, and three differences
follow from that.

\textbf{Continuous dates versus categorical assignment.}  The Higher Criticism
method assigns each text to the most likely of three corpora.  However, D and
the Deuteronomistic History are both dated to the late monarchic or exilic
period, so two texts composed at 650 and 590~BCE receive identical labels, and
no intra-school temporal resolution is possible.  The model used here returns a
date with a calibrated interval, recovering whatever temporal resolution the
data support and quantifying the rest as uncertainty.

\textbf{Period features versus topic features.}  Faigenbaum-Golovin et al.\
operate on lemma and lemma n-gram frequencies, a representation in which
content words --- \textit{gold} in Tabernacle chapters, \textit{king} in
regnal narratives --- dominate.  Content-word frequency is sensitive to topic
and genre as much as to date.  The feature set here is deliberately dominated
by high-frequency grammatical rates (verbal aspect and stem distributions,
part-of-speech transition rates, clause-relation profiles) that vary with
period rather than subject matter.  This is what permits comparison of poetry
against narrative, which a bag-of-words representation cannot do.

\textbf{An explicit accounting of archaizing.}  Attribution methods offer no
mechanism for telling a genuinely ancient text from one composed in a
deliberately archaic register.  A Persian-period author who archaizes to D
norms will be assigned to D regardless of when he wrote.  Rather than claim
immunity from the problem, the sensitivity is tested directly below.  In Greek,
where the archaizing is real and its authors are known, it is measured and it is
large.  In Hebrew the test returns a non-detection: the displacement produced by
substituting the recognized diagnostic vocabulary is well below this model's
noise floor, so the honest report is that archaizing of that kind cannot be
detected here rather than that it is cheap.

These are differences of purpose rather than deficiencies in either approach.
The ideal treatment of a disputed text would apply both, as attribution output
can set register priors while date estimates constrain the plausible settings
for an attribution decision.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Data: Corpus and Feature Extraction}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{The BHSA Database}

All Hebrew analysis uses the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia Amstelodamensis
(\bhsa{}) database~\cite{BHSA2021}, accessed through
Text-Fabric~\cite{Roorda2018}.  Extraction is restricted to words that \bhsa{}
marks as Hebrew, which matters more than it sounds: Ezra 4:8--6:18 and 7:12--26
are Aramaic and account for \arwEzra\% of that book, and Jer~10:11 adds a
further \arwJer{} words.  Daniel's Aramaic section, 2:4b--7:28, is excluded by
the chapter range assigned to that unit.  \bhsa{} supplies a complete morphological and
syntactic annotation of the Masoretic text: for every word, a lexeme
identifier, part of speech, verbal tense/aspect and stem, person, number,
gender, pronominal suffix and state; and for every phrase and clause, a type,
a syntactic function, and a relation to its governing clause.  These
annotations are the product of decades of work by the Eep Talstra Centre for
Bible and Computer and are independent of any dating hypothesis.

\subsection*{The Anchored Corpus}

The training corpus comprises \HBbooks{} units spanning \HBoldest--\HBlatest{}
BCE, listed in Table~\ref{tab:corpus}.  Books with disputed internal composition
histories are split into the conventional scholarly divisions (Isaiah into
three, Zechariah into two), and the oracular core of Jeremiah is separated from
its Deuteronomistic prose frame, which is treated as an undated target rather
than an anchor.

The units differ in the kind of evidence that fixes their dates, and the
difference is marked in the table along the lines set out above.  Twelve carry an
explicit synchronism and twelve a datable historical referent, neither of which
depends on the feature cline under analysis.  Jonah alone is dated principally
by typology, following the critical commentary~\cite{Wolff1986}, with some
recent work pressing it later still~\cite{Dell1996}; even there a terminus post
quem is available, since Nineveh is described as a city that already lay in
ruins (Jonah 3:3).

Table~\ref{tab:anchors} reports how much any of this matters.  A
leave-one-unit-out jackknife, re-running the entire pipeline 25 times, gives a
rank correlation between $\JKrhomin$ and $\JKrhomax$ with a median of
$\JKrhomed$, and pairwise accuracy between \JKpairmin\% and \JKpairmax\%.
That spread is the leverage a single unit carries at this corpus size, and it
falls almost entirely on the late anchors that fix the recent end of the scale:
removing Nehemiah, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, or Jonah each costs between \JKcostMin{} and
\JKcostMid{} of correlation, while removing any pre-exilic unit costs at most 0.05.  The
full-corpus figure of $\HBrho$ should accordingly be read against that range
rather than as a point estimate.

Removing the less securely anchored units changes little.  Dropping all six that
lack an explicit synchronism leaves $\rho$ at \ANCrho{} with a mean absolute error
of \ANCmae~yr against a \ANCbase~yr baseline, better in both respects than the full
corpus.  Dropping Jonah and Ecclesiastes together costs \JKcostMax{} of correlation,
which is what dropping any two late anchors costs and is not peculiar to them.

What matters more than whether the anchors might be wrong is which way being
wrong would push the results, and that is not symmetric.  The model learns its
mapping from language to date from the anchors, so an anchor whose true date is
\emph{later} than the date assigned to it teaches the model to associate that
book's linguistic profile with too early a date, and the error is carried into
every target whose language resembles it.  Anchor error propagates to the
targets with the same sign.

Displacing the whole chronology \ABshift~yr toward the present and re-running
the estimator moves the three sources by \ABAllJE, \ABAllD{} and \ABAllP~yr:
pass-through is \ABpass\% and one for one.  Confining the displacement to the
six anchors that lack an external synchronism---the case where the securely
fixed dates are right and only the judgment calls are wrong---moves them by at
most \ABsoftMax~yr, so the units whose dating is most open to argument carry
correspondingly little of the result.  Displacing only the post-exilic anchors
moves the sources \ABLateJE, \ABLateD{} and \ABLateP~yr, slightly more than the
displacement applied, since it is the late anchors that fix where late-looking
targets land.

The direction of any likely error therefore matters, and it is worth stating
which way the field has been moving.  A century of critical work has revised
biblical dates later, not earlier, and the recent archaeological
argument~\cite{Adler2022} runs the same way.  If the anchors used here are
systematically wrong, they are more probably assigned too early than too late.
Since the conclusion drawn below is that the Pentateuchal sources are
\emph{late}, an anchor chronology erring early makes that conclusion
conservative: correcting it would move the sources later still.  The error that
would threaten the conclusion is the opposite one, and it is the less likely of
the two.  This is an argument about direction, not a correction, and no
adjustment is applied anywhere in what follows.

\subsection*{Why Passages Rather Than Books}

The most consequential design choice in this article is that features are
extracted from passages of about \HBtarget{} words rather than from whole books.

At the level of whole books the corpus offers only \HBbooks{} observations.  Any
feature set large enough to describe Hebrew morphosyntax then has more
dimensions than there are data points.  The standard responses to this ---
screening features by their correlation with date, or reducing dimension using
the date labels --- both consult the labels before cross-validation and thereby
inflate apparent performance.  Worse, a whole-book rate is a single number
summarizing tens of thousands of words, so a book whose passages are internally
consistent cannot be told apart from one that is a composite.

Partitioning at $\sim$\HBtarget{} words yields \HBchunks{} passages from the same
\HBwords{} words.  This is not a free multiplication of the sample size.
Passages from one book are correlated, so the appropriate measure is the
effective sample size $n_{\mathrm{eff}} = n / (1 + (\bar{m}-1)\rho_{I})$, where
$\rho_I$ is the intraclass correlation and $\bar m$ the mean number of passages
per book.  Across passage sizes from \ICCszLo{} to \ICCszHi{} words the median
intraclass correlation runs \ICClo--\ICChi, and the effective sample size is
\ICCgainLo{} to \ICCgainHi{} times the book-level figure (S2 Table).  That is the real gain, and it is what
makes a feature set of this width estimable at all.

Passage size trades two effects against each other.  Smaller passages give more
observations but sparser features, since a lexical item occurring once per
thousand words will be absent from most 200-word passages, and its rate is then
not a measurement but a coin flip.  Larger passages give denser features but
fewer observations.  I therefore crossed passage sizes of 200, 300, 400, 500, 700, and 1000 words
with three feature sets and with calibration on and off, 36 configurations in
all, selecting on out-of-sample rank correlation under leave-one-book-out
(S3 Table).  The selected configuration uses $\sim$500-word
passages, though performance is flat between 400 and 1000, so the choice is not
a delicate one.

Passages respect verse boundaries: words are accumulated verse by verse until
the target is reached.  A trailing remainder shorter than half the target is
merged into the preceding passage rather than kept as a short, high-variance
observation.  The resulting passages are close to the nominal size, from
\cszMin{} to \cszMax{} words with a median of \cszMed{} and \cszBand\% falling
between 400 and 700.  Two units, Obadiah and Nahum, are short enough to yield a
single passage and are therefore book-level observations; their
passage-level dispersion in Table~\ref{tab:lobo} is zero for that reason rather
than because they are homogeneous.

Cutting at verse boundaries also makes the phrase- and clause-level features
well defined.  Those features are collected over every phrase and clause
overlapping a passage, so an object straddling a boundary would be counted in
both neighbors and its type credited to each.  In \bhsa{} this scarcely
happens: across the whole database only 0.01\% of phrases and 0.06\% of clauses
span a verse boundary, and in the \HBchunks{} passages of the training corpus
the number of partially contained phrases and clauses is \bndPhr{} and \bndCl{}
respectively.  Sentences are the exception, spanning verses in 1.4\% of cases
overall and leaving \bndSent{} partially contained passages here
(\bndSentPct\%), which biases the mean sentence length by $-0.2$\%.

\subsection*{Feature Extraction}

The feature set is fixed by frequency rank computed over the whole \bhsa{}
corpus, without reference to date.  \Fextract{} features are extracted, of which
\Fdead{} are structurally constant on this corpus and are dropped inside each
fold, leaving \HBfeat{} in six families:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Lexical rates} (\Flex{} features): occurrences per 1000 words of
    each of the 250 most frequent lexemes in the corpus.  Since selection goes
    by corpus frequency, these are dominated by function words --- articles,
    prepositions, conjunctions, pronouns --- rather than by the rare
    diagnostic vocabulary of the \cbh{}/\lbh{} literature.  This is deliberate,
    as the sparsity constraint above rules out the rare items, and the
    consequences of that are taken up below.
  \item \textbf{Part-of-speech transition rates} (\Fpos{} features): rates of each
    ordered pair of parts of speech across adjacent words, capturing local
    syntactic profile without reference to any particular construction.
  \item \textbf{Verb morphology} (\Fverb{} features): distributions over tense/aspect
    (qatal, yiqtol, wayyiqtol, participle, infinitive, imperative), stem (qal,
    nifal, piel, hifil, hitpael, pual, hofal), and their interaction.
  \item \textbf{Phrase and clause structure} (\Fphr{} features): phrase type and
    syntactic function rates, and clause-relation rates from the \bhsa{}
    clause hierarchy.
  \item \textbf{Agreement and suffix morphology} (\Fagr{} features): person, number,
    gender and pronominal-suffix rates.
  \item \textbf{Structural} (\Fstruct{} features): mean phrase and clause length,
    clauses per passage, and type--token ratio.
\end{enumerate}

Two extensions were built and evaluated and neither is used.  A character and
part-of-speech n-gram extension adding \NGfeat{} further features does not improve
out-of-sample performance at the selected passage size (S3 Table).  A
clause-type family --- rates and transition rates over the \bhsa{} clause types
that encode the Hebrew verbal system, including the wayyiqtol narrative clause
(Way0) and the weqatal clause (WQt0) --- was added after an audit found that an
earlier implementation had counted clause types while indexing them by clause
relation, whose value sets are disjoint, so that the family had been silently
absent.  Implemented correctly, its members are among the most strongly
date-correlated single features in the corpus: \CTYPnHalf{} of the \CTYPnAll{}
clause types correlate with true date above $|\rho| = 0.5$ at book level, led by
\CTYPtopName{} at $\CTYPtopRho$ and \CTYPsecName{} at $\CTYPsecRho$.  And yet
adding all \CTYPfeat{} of them
leaves out-of-sample performance unchanged ($\rho$ \CTYPrhoBefore{} to
\CTYPrhoAfter, mean absolute error \CTYPmaeBefore{} to \CTYPmaeAfter~yr).  Their information is already carried by the
verb-morphology and part-of-speech transition features.  The reported model is
therefore the one without them, and the exercise is reported because it
indicates the feature set is saturated rather than arbitrary.

Features whose standard deviation is zero on the training fold, or which are
missing in more than 20\% of passages, are dropped inside the fold.  Remaining
missing values are imputed at the training-fold median.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Model}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{Weighted Ridge Regression}

Let $\mathbf{X}$ be the $n \times p$ matrix of passage features and
$\mathbf{y}$ the vector of book dates, each passage inheriting its book's
date.  Features are centered and scaled on the training fold.  The estimator is
ridge regression,
\begin{equation}
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
  = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}
    \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i \left( y_i - \mathbf{x}_i^{\!\top}\boldsymbol\beta \right)^2
    + \lambda \|\boldsymbol\beta\|^2 ,
\end{equation}
solved in dual form, $\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} =
\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\!\top} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}
\tilde{\mathbf{y}}$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is the weighted standardized design.
Because $p > n$ on the Hebrew side, the dual form is the cheaper route, and
one eigendecomposition of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\!\top}$ serves the entire
$\lambda$ sweep.  $\lambda$ is selected by an inner leave-one-book-out loop
nested inside each outer fold, never using the held-out book.

\subsection*{Inverse-Density Weighting}

The anchored corpus is not uniform in time.  Post-exilic material outnumbers
pre-exilic material, and an unweighted fit is pulled toward the dense region:
in the unweighted model no book receives a confidently pre-exilic estimate,
which is a property of the sampling rather than of Hebrew.  Weights are
therefore taken inversely proportional to a kernel estimate of the date
density,
\begin{equation}
w_i \propto \left[ \sum_j \exp\!\left( -\tfrac{1}{2}
  \left( \frac{d_j - d_i}{h} \right)^{\!2} \right) \right]^{-\alpha} ,
\end{equation}
with bandwidth $h = 90$~yr and exponent $\alpha = 1$, normalized to mean one.
Weighted ridge is implemented as ordinary ridge on rows scaled by
$\sqrt{w_i}$.

\subsection*{Variance Matching and Its Cost}

A regularized regression is a shrinkage estimator, so its predictions have
systematically smaller variance than the quantity being predicted.  Under plain
ridge, the predicted dates for the anchored corpus span roughly a third of the
true range, and no text can then be assigned a confidently early or confidently
late date.  This is an artifact of shrinkage rather than a finding about
Hebrew.  The correction is to match the first two moments of the out-of-sample
predictions to the true dates,
\begin{equation}
\hat{d} \;=\; \bar{d} \;+\; S\,(\hat{d}_{\text{raw}} - \bar{d}_{\text{raw}}),
\qquad
S = \frac{\mathrm{sd}(d)}{\mathrm{sd}(\hat{d}_{\text{raw}})},
\end{equation}
with $\bar d$, $\mathrm{sd}(d)$, $\bar d_{\text{raw}}$ and $S$ all computed
from leave-one-book-out predictions on the training corpus only.  Here
$S = \HBscale$.  The step is the inverse-calibration correction familiar from
the classical-versus-inverse regression literature~\cite{Krutchkoff1967}: when
the object is to recover the predictor rather than to minimize squared error in
the response, matching the spread of the estimates to the spread of the
quantity being estimated is the appropriate adjustment.

This is a deliberate trade, and both sides of it ought to be stated.  Rescaling
\emph{increases} the mean absolute error, since inflating the spread of the
predictions amplifies their errors along with their signal: the uncalibrated
model gives \UNCALmae~yr against \HBmae~yr for the rescaled one.  What the
trade buys is a model that is two-sided.  Uncalibrated predictions span only
\UNCALspan~yr against \TRUEspan~yr of real dates and place just \UNCALpreok{}
of the \HBnpre{} genuinely pre-exilic books before the exile.  After rescaling,
the predictions span \VARspan~yr and \HBnpreok{} of \HBnpre{} are placed
correctly.

Because the substantive question in the Pentateuchal debate is which side of
the exile a text falls on, a model that can hardly ever say ``early'' is
useless for that purpose whatever its mean absolute error.  Its inability to
say ``early'' is a property of the estimator, not evidence that nothing is
early.  Readers whose interest is point accuracy rather than calibration should
use the uncalibrated variant, whose figures are in S3 Table.

\subsection*{Computational Reproducibility}

The analysis is a single pipeline of \NPipeStages{} stages, run by one script,
in dependency order: corpus extraction from \bhsa{}, feature construction,
validation, the permutation nulls, the undated predictions, and every robustness
analysis reported below.  No number in this article is now produced by hand or
at an interactive prompt; that this was not always true is the subject of the
third paragraph.

Two properties are enforced, not merely claimed.  First, every quantity in the
text is a macro read from a result file at build time; a missing result file
fails the build instead of leaving a stale figure in place, and a mechanical
check refuses to compile the manuscript if any number appears in the prose that
did not come from a result file.  Second, the pipeline records a cryptographic
digest of each of its \NPipeOutputs{} outputs and compares them on the next run,
so that a change anywhere becomes visible at once, not at the next reading.

Running the pipeline twice from the corpus reproduces all \NPipeOutputs{}
outputs byte for byte.  Achieving that required fixing three defects that a
casual re-run would not have exposed: a feature matrix that no longer matched
the extractor that had supposedly produced it, three result files that had been
generated at an interactive prompt and never committed, and a permutation
checkpoint that survived a corpus rebuild and was silently reused against a
model it no longer described.  Each is the kind of error that changes published
numbers without changing anything a reader can see.  Long-running stages now
record a fingerprint of their inputs beside their checkpoint and refuse to
resume across a mismatch.

The verification log is included in the repository.  Readers should note that
reproducing the permutation nulls takes several hours; every other stage
completes in about fifteen minutes.

\subsection*{Jackknife+ Prediction Intervals}

Split conformal prediction assumes that every calibration residual comes from a
single fitted model, on data exchangeable with the target~\cite{Vovk2005,Lei2018}.
That assumption does not hold here.  Each residual in this design comes from a
\emph{different} model, fitted without its own book, which makes the procedure
a jackknife rather than split conformal, and naive jackknife intervals carry no
finite-sample guarantee.  Intervals are therefore built by the jackknife+ of
Barber et al.~\cite{Barber2021}.  Writing $\mu_{-i}$ for the model fitted
without book $i$ and $R_i$ for that book's leave-one-out residual, the interval
for a target $x$ is
\begin{equation}
\Big[\; q^{-}_{\alpha}\{\mu_{-i}(x) - R_i\},\;\;
        q^{+}_{1-\alpha}\{\mu_{-i}(x) + R_i\} \;\Big],
\end{equation}
which is distribution-free and has finite-sample coverage of at least
$1-2\alpha$.  The price of the guarantee is that a nominal 90\% interval is
warranted only to 80\% and a nominal 68\% interval only to 36\%; empirical
coverage on the anchored corpus is \covsixeight\% and \covninety\%
respectively, so in practice the intervals are conservative rather than
optimistic.

The variance-matching constants are recomputed inside each fold, so that
$\mu_{-i}$ and $R_i$ are free of the book being predicted.  Estimating them
once on all \HBbooks{} leave-one-out predictions, as an earlier version did,
understates the mean absolute error by about ten years and narrows the
68\% half-width from \qnestedsixeight{} to \HBqsixeight~yr.  Rank correlation
and pairwise ordering are unaffected either way, since the rescaling is a
positive linear map.

For a target unit, $P(\text{post-exilic})$ is the fraction of the jackknife+
ensemble $\{\mu_{-i}(x) \pm R_i\}$ falling after 586~BCE.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Validation}
\label{sec:validation}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{A Failure Mode That Inflates Reported Accuracy}

Reported accuracies for linguistic dating models of this class vary by two
orders of magnitude.  Much of that variation is not a difference in the
underlying signal but an artifact of how the models are validated, and the
artifact is worth naming because it is easy to commit and hard to see.

In a Bayesian dating model, the posterior over a held-out text's date combines
a likelihood from the linguistic features with a prior.  Should the prior for
the held-out text be centered on that text's own scholarly date, which is the
natural thing to do when the prior is meant to encode what scholars think, then
the model is being asked to recover a number it has already been handed.  The
resulting holdout error measures the width of the prior rather than the
information in the language.

The effect is large.  Under a prior-centered design on this corpus, the median
share of posterior precision contributed by the linguistic evidence is
\leakShare\%, and mean holdout error is \leakLeaky~yr.  Under an agnostic
prior with an otherwise identical pipeline, the same model achieves
\leakHonest~yr.  For the \leakTightN{} units whose scholarly dates carry the
tightest uncertainty ($\sigma \leq 20$~yr), the linguistic evidence supplies
\leakTightShare\% of posterior precision and the leaky design reports
\leakTightLeaky~yr against an honest \leakTightHonest~yr
(Table~\ref{tab:leakage}).  For a model of this kind, a reported accuracy of a
decade or two is a signature of the design rather than an achievement.

\input{tables/tab_leakage}

All results below use an agnostic prior; the reported model is not Bayesian
and has no prior to leak.

\subsection*{The Leave-One-Book-Out Protocol}

Cross-validation folds are whole books, never passages.  Passages from one book
are strongly correlated, so splitting them across a fold boundary would let the
model see the held-out book's own material.  Within each fold, and using only
the training books, features with zero variance or excessive missingness are
dropped, medians for imputation are computed, standardization constants are
computed, inverse-density weights are computed, $\lambda$ is selected by an
inner leave-one-book-out loop, and the variance-matching constants and
jackknife+ residuals are derived.  The held-out book's date is used only to
score the result.

A book's estimate is the median of its passage estimates.  The dispersion of
those passage estimates is reported separately (Table~\ref{tab:lobo}) and is
informative in its own right, being small for compositionally uniform books and
large for composites.

\subsection*{What the Signal Supports}

\input{tables/tab_lobo}

Under this protocol the model achieves a mean absolute error of \HBmae~yr,
against \HBmaebase~yr for the constant predictor that assigns every book the
corpus mean date.  Rank correlation between true and estimated date is
$\HBrho$ ($p = \HBrhop$), and \HBpair\% of the \HBnpair{} book pairs are
placed in the correct chronological order.

However, the same corpus was used to choose the passage size and feature set,
so parametric $p$-values would be optimistic.  Significance is therefore
established by a permutation null in which book dates are shuffled and the
\emph{entire} pipeline is re-run --- weighting, $\lambda$ selection, variance
matching and all --- \HBnperm{} times.  Permutation is at book level, not
passage level, so the clustering structure is preserved under the null; a
passage-level shuffle would break the correlation between passages of the same
book and produce a null that is far too easy to beat.  Against this null the
observed rank correlation of $\HBrho$ has $p = \HBpermrho$ (null median
$\HBnullrho$), the pairwise ordering accuracy of \HBpair\% has $p =
\HBpermpair$ (null median \HBnullpair\%), and the mean absolute error of
\HBmae~yr has $p = \HBpermmae$ (null median \HBnullmae~yr).

One arithmetic point deserves emphasis, since pairwise ordering accuracy is
commonly reported in this literature without it.  The \HBnpair{} pairs formed
from \HBbooks{} books are not independent, as each book appears in
\HBbooks$-1$ of them.  Treating the accuracy as a binomial proportion over
\HBnpair{} independent trials gives $p$-values wrong by ten orders of magnitude.
The permutation figures above are the correct ones, and any comparison with
pairwise accuracies reported elsewhere should take this into account.

\subsection*{Genre Is the Dominant Confound}

The rank correlation just reported is not what it appears to be, and the
correction is large enough that reporting the raw figure alone would be
misleading.

The anchored corpus is \GNnProph{} prophetic books, \GNnNar{} narrative books,
and one book each of poetry, wisdom and apocalyptic.  Residuals are strongly
structured by genre: narrative books are placed \GNoffNar~yr from their true
dates on average and prophetic books \GNoffPro~yr.  \GNbetween\% of the
variance in the model's predictions lies between genres rather than within
them.

This could be an artifact of where the genres sit on the timeline, since all
\GNnNar{} narrative anchors are post-exilic.  The test that separates the two
is a date-matched contrast.  Among anchors written between \GNwinHi{} and
\GNwinLo~BCE, where both genres are represented, narrative residuals average
\GNwinNar~yr and prophetic residuals \GNwinPro~yr, a difference of
\GNwinDiff~yr (Welch $t = \GNwinT$, $p = \GNwinP$).  Regressing residual on
true date across all narrative and prophetic anchors, the narrative indicator
is \GNregNar~yr ($t = \GNregT$, $p = \GNregP$).  The effect is genre, not the
endpoint.

The consequence is that raw rank correlation overstates the chronological
signal.  Centering both truth and prediction within genre, the correlation
falls from $\GNrhoRaw$ to $\GNrhoPartial$.  Within the \GNnProph{} prophetic
books alone---a single register spanning \GNprophHi{} to \GNprophLo~BCE, the
best-controlled comparison this corpus permits---it is $\GNrhoProph$ ($p =
\GNpProph$).  Both figures are reported throughout in preference to the raw
one.

Whether anything survives the confound is a question a permutation null can
answer, provided the null is the right one.  A null that shuffles dates freely
destroys the genre--date association along with the chronology, and so tests
only whether the model can tell genres apart, which it plainly can.  The
appropriate null is restricted: dates are permuted only \emph{within} genre, so
the genre--date association this corpus happens to contain is preserved exactly
and only the within-genre chronology is destroyed.  Against \GNnullN{} such
permutations, each a complete re-run of the pipeline, the observed
genre-controlled correlation of $\GNrhoPartial$ has $p = \GNnullP$ (null median
$\GNnullMed$).  A chronological signal survives the confound, and it is that
signal, not the raw correlation, that the results below rest on.

\subsection*{The Signal Is Lexical, Not Morphosyntactic}

The features fall into two families: \LXnlex{} lexeme frequencies, and
\RTBfeat{} morphosyntactic features covering verb stem and tense, clause type
and relation, phrase structure, agreement and suffixation.  Refitting on each
family separately settles which carries the result, and the answer is
one-sided.

On the morphosyntactic features alone, genre-controlled $\rho$ is
$\RTBgenre$ and within-prophecy $\rho$ is $\RTBproph$.  On the lexemes alone it
is $\RTCgenre$ and $\RTCproph$, marginally better than the full feature set.
Grammatical change over this period, as encoded in the \bhsa{} annotation and
measured across \HBbooks{} books, is not detectable by this model.  Whatever
diachrony the model uses is vocabulary.

That is not by itself an objection.  Lexical replacement is the backbone of the
existing method~\cite{Hurvitz1982}, and Persian loanwords and Aramaisms are its
standard evidence.  But it invites a sharper one: a model keyed to vocabulary
may be detecting subject matter rather than date, and the highest-leverage
lexemes include \emph{Israel}, \emph{Jacob}, YHWH and \emph{holy}.

Two checks argue against that reading.  First, high-leverage lexemes are only
weakly more genre-diagnostic than low-leverage ones---across the \LXnlex{}
lexemes, leverage correlates with genre $\eta^2$ at $\LXrhoEta$, and the fifty
highest-leverage lexemes average \LXetaTop{} against \LXetaBot{} for the fifty
lowest.  Topic discrimination is too weak to account for a signal this size.

Second, and more directly: the model recovers the textbook first-person pronoun
shift unprompted.  Of the recognized CBH/LBH diagnostic lexemes, only
\LXdiagPresent{} of \LXdiagTotal{} are frequent enough to survive the frequency
filter---the Persian loans and Aramaisms that constitute the strongest evidence
in the literature are all too rare---and both that do survive rank in the top
fifth by leverage, at a median rank of \LXdiagRank{} of \LXnlex.  They are the
two members of one pair.  Classical \emph{'an\=ok\^\i}{} ranks
\LXanokiRank{} and pushes estimates earlier; late \emph{'\u{a}n\^\i}{}
ranks \LXaniRank{} and pushes them later.  That is the direction the literature
predicts, learned from dated books without any encoding of the pair.  A topic
classifier has no reason to place those two words high and in opposition.

\subsection*{Correcting for the Configuration Search}

The figures above come from a configuration --- passage size, weighting
exponent, ridge penalty --- that was itself chosen by comparing out-of-sample
performance across a search on this same corpus.  A permutation null that holds
the winning configuration fixed does not account for that choice, so the
reported correlation is the maximum over a search and is optimistic by an
unknown amount.

The amount can be measured by nesting the search.  For each held-out book, the
entire configuration was selected by an inner leave-one-book-out loop over the
remaining 24 units, drawn from a grid of \NSgrid{} combinations, and only then
was the held-out book predicted.  Nothing about the configuration is informed by
the book being scored.

Under that protocol the mean absolute error is \NSmae~yr against \HBmaebase~yr
for the constant predictor, the rank correlation is $\NSrho$ ($p = \NSrhop$),
pairwise ordering is \NSpair\%, and \NSside{} of \HBbooks{} books fall on the
correct side of the exile.  Selection therefore inflates the rank correlation by
\SELinflate{} and the pairwise accuracy by \SELinflatePair{} points.  The attenuated
figures are the ones a fresh corpus should be expected to reproduce, and the
substantive conclusions do not depend on the difference.  The search is also
stable: the same weighting exponent is chosen in 24 of the 25 folds, and the
passage size alternates between the two adjacent settings whose performance the
sweep found indistinguishable.

Variance matching is excluded from this grid deliberately.  It is a positive
linear map of the predictions, so it leaves both the rank correlation and the
pairwise ordering exactly unchanged and cannot inflate either.  It is applied
always, as an a priori correction for shrinkage of the kind long used in
inverse calibration~\cite{Krutchkoff1967}, rather than tuned for performance.

\subsection*{Two-Sidedness and Calibration}

What matters for the Pentateuchal application is whether the model can say
``early'' as well as ``late''.  After inverse-density weighting and variance
matching, \HBnpreok{} of the \HBnpre{} genuinely pre-exilic books are placed
before 586~BCE, and \HBnpostok{} of the \HBnpost{} post-exilic ones after it, giving \HBsideok{} of \HBbooks{} overall (Table~\ref{tab:lobo}).
Without those two steps the model places almost nothing before the exile, and
its apparent confidence that everything is late is an artifact of how the
corpus is distributed in time rather than evidence about any text.

Fig~\ref{fig:calibration} shows estimated against true date with the jackknife+
bands.  Empirical coverage of the nominal 68\% band is slightly conservative,
which is the expected behavior of jackknife+ intervals at this sample size.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\textwidth]{figures/fig_calibration.pdf}
\caption{{\bf Leave-one-book-out calibration.}  Each point is one anchored
book, dated by a model fitted without it.  The dashed line is exact recovery;
shaded bands are the 68\% and 90\% jackknife+ intervals.  Books whose estimate
falls on the wrong side of the exile are marked with diamonds.  Standardization,
weighting, regularization and interval calibration were all performed inside
the fold.}
\label{fig:calibration}
\end{figure}

\subsection*{What the Signal Does Not Support}

Three limits ought to be stated in the same breath as the results.

First, \HBmae~yr against a \HBmaebase~yr baseline is a real improvement but a
modest one.  What the model provides is a chronological \emph{ordering} that has
been calibrated onto an absolute scale, not a precise clock.  The reported
intervals of $\pm\HBqsixeight$~yr at 68\% express as much.

Second, the largest single error is \HBworstbook{} at \HBworsterr~yr.  Genre
drives most of this, as narrative books are placed late and poetic books early
relative to their true dates (see below).  Any single estimate for a text of
unusual genre should be read accordingly.

Third, nothing here resolves dates \emph{within} the post-exilic period.  A text
estimated at 380~BCE with a $\pm\HBqsixeight$~yr interval cannot be
distinguished from one estimated at 300~BCE.  The claims that follow are
therefore confined to the pre-exilic/post-exilic distinction and to relative
ordering, both of which the validation supports.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Results: Within the Sources}
\label{sec:results}
% =====================================================================

The model, fitted on all \HBbooks{} anchored books, was applied to
\NTargets{} undated units: the three classical documentary sources, their
conventional sub-strata, the five Pentateuchal books as received, the
Deuteronomistic prose of Jeremiah, and the three archaic poems.  Source
partitions follow the standard critical division at chapter granularity,
specified in S1 Appendix.  Chapter granularity is exact for the sub-strata,
whose ranges partition their parent sources without remainder, and nearly so for
the three sources: Genesis 6 and 25, where the Priestly and JE material is
interwoven verse by verse, are the only chapters assigned to two sources.  No
target contributed to training, feature selection, weighting, regularization or
calibration.

This section asks what the model sees inside a source rather than where it
places the source as a whole.  Two quantities are available.  Dispersion---how
widely a source's own passages scatter---is invariant to the calibration, since
variance matching multiplies every prediction by one positive constant and so
leaves the ordering of units by dispersion unchanged.  Separation between a
source's conventional blocks is not invariant in that way, and turns out not to
be invariant to the genre control either.  The first survives in part and the
second does not, and both are reported.

\subsection*{The Sources Differ in How Internally Varied They Are}

Each source is made of many \HBtarget-word passages, and each passage receives
its own estimate (Fig~\ref{fig:layers}, Table~\ref{tab:layers}).  If a source is a single composition, its passages should
scatter about as widely as the passages of a single dated book do.  If it is a
rolling document---an older core with later accretion---it should scatter more.

The yardstick is the anchored corpus itself.  Across the \LYrefN{} anchor books
with at least four passages, the within-book standard deviation of passage
estimates has a median of \LYrefMed~yr.  That figure is generous to the
sources rather than harsh on them, because several anchors are themselves
composite; Isaiah 1--39 is the obvious case.

Dispersion rises with the number of passages a unit contains ($\rho = \LYsizeRho$
across the anchors, $p = \LYsizeP$), and the three sources contain \LYJEn, \LYDn{}
and \LYPn{} passages, so the comparison is made at matched count.  Subsampling
each source to \LYDn{} passages, the standard deviation of passage estimates is
\LYJEsd~yr for the JE composite, \LYPsd~yr for P and \LYDsd~yr for D.  The
ordering is \LYorder.  Bootstrapping over passages, $P(\mathrm{SD}_{JE} >
\mathrm{SD}_{D}) = \LYpJEgtD$, $P(\mathrm{SD}_{JE} > \mathrm{SD}_{P}) =
\LYpJEgtP$ and $P(\mathrm{SD}_{D} > \mathrm{SD}_{P}) = \LYpDgtP$.

Only part of that ordering is robust.  Applying the genre screen described in
the Validation section, D remains the least dispersed of the three at every
screen level, with $P(\mathrm{SD}_{JE} > \mathrm{SD}_{D})$ never falling below
\DRminJEgtD.  A source usually described as layered is, by this measure, the
tidiest one in the Pentateuch, and that holds however hard the genre-diagnostic
features are screened out.

The rank of JE does not hold.  Unscreened, JE is the most varied of the three,
at the \LYJEpct{}th percentile of single dated books.  With a quarter of the
genre-diagnostic features removed, P overtakes it
($P(\mathrm{SD}_{JE} > \mathrm{SD}_{P}) = \DRQpJEgtP$), and with half removed
the comparison is a coin flip (\DRHpJEgtP).  Screening also inflates every
dispersion---JE rises from \DRFullJE{} to \DRHJE~yr and P from \DRFullP{} to
\DRHP---because half as many features make a noisier estimate, so some of this
is lost power rather than a changed answer.  Either way the evidence does not
distinguish JE from P, and the claim that JE is the most heterogeneous of the
three sources is not supported.  What survives is that D is the least.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/fig_layers.pdf}
\caption{{\bf Passage-level estimates within each source.}  One point per
\HBtarget-word passage; bars are interquartile ranges and the rule is the
median.  Sub-blocks are indented beneath their source.  The shaded band is
pre-exilic.  Dispersion within a source and separation between its blocks are
different measurements.  The separations between blocks shown here do not
survive a genre control and are discussed as register effects in the text;
the dispersion ordering is robust only for D.}
\label{fig:layers}
\end{figure}

\input{tables/tab_layers}

\subsection*{The Apparent Block Separations Are Register, Not Date}

Splitting each source at the division its critical literature already draws
produces a striking result that does not survive inspection.  I report it, and
its failure, because the failure is the more useful of the two.

On the full feature set the blocks separate cleanly and in the expected
direction.  The law code of Deuteronomy 12--26 is placed \BRFullDCodegap~yr
earlier than the surrounding frame of chapters 1--11 and 27--34 (95\% CI
\BRFullDCodelo{} to \BRFullDCodehi, Mann--Whitney $p = \BRFullDCodep$).  The
Holiness Code separates from the Priestly material of Leviticus 1--16 by
\BRFullHolgap~yr ($p = \BRFullHolp$), and the JE material of Genesis from that
of Exodus by \BRFullGenJEgap~yr ($p = \BRFullGenJEp$).  None of those
boundaries was supplied to the model, which received chapter ranges and nothing
else, and all three point the way two centuries of literary criticism would
predict.

The Validation section, however, establishes that genre is the dominant axis of
variation in this corpus, and that screening out the most genre-diagnostic
features improves the model's ability to order the anchors once genre is held
fixed.  Applying that same screen to the block comparisons dissolves them
(Table~\ref{tab:s11}).  With the most genre-diagnostic quarter of the features
removed, the Deuteronomic separation falls to \BRQDCodegap~yr ($p =
\BRQDCodep$) and neither of the others remains significant.  With half removed,
at the screen level that gives the \emph{best} genre-controlled ordering
($\rho = \BRHrho$ against $\BRFullrho$ unscreened), the Deuteronomic
separation is \BRHDCodegap~yr---reversed, and significant in the opposite
direction ($p = \BRHDCodep$).

The specification curve shows the same thing from the other side: across the
\SPcodeN{} validated specifications the law code is placed earlier than the
frame in only \SPcodeEarlier, and the direction tracks the feature screen
almost perfectly.

The reading that fits is unwelcome and simple.  The law code is legal prose and
the frame is hortatory narrative; the Holiness Code and the Priestly material of
Leviticus differ likewise in register.  The apparent chronological gap between
them was carried by the vocabulary that distinguishes those registers, and when
that vocabulary is removed the gap goes with it.  These are register effects,
not dates.

Two things are worth saying about this.  The first is that the loss of
significance in the Holiness and JE comparisons is partly a loss of power:
screening halves the feature count and the intervals widen accordingly.  The
Deuteronomic reversal is not that---a sign flip significant at $p =
\BRHDCodep$ is not what attenuation looks like.

The second is that this is what a genre control is for.  A study that reported
the unscreened numbers, which are individually significant and align with prior
expectation, would have produced three publishable claims and three false ones.
The screen that the anchored corpus forces on the dating results turns out to be
load-bearing here too, and any future attempt to detect compositional strata
this way will have to clear the same bar.  Detecting internal structure by
linguistic date remains a reasonable ambition; \HBbooks{} anchor books spanning
a single religious literature are not enough to do it.

\subsection*{Three Sources of Variance, and Their Sizes}

It is worth stating plainly how the uncertainties in this study compare, since
they are easily conflated.  The model's own uncertainty is much the largest:
the 68\% jackknife+ interval has a half-width of roughly \SPPhalf~yr for each
source.  Within-source heterogeneity is next, at \LYDsd--\LYJEsd~yr.  The
instability of the estimate across analytic specifications is the smallest of
the three, at \SPDspecsd--\SPPspecsd~yr (below).

The sources are more internally variable than the analysis is unstable.  A
single date for a source made of passages spanning a century or more was never
a well-defined quantity to estimate, and this is the reason estimates of it
move when the specification moves.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Results: Placement Relative to the Exile}
\label{sec:placement}
% =====================================================================

Absolute dates are the weaker half of this study, and I report them in the form
the evidence supports: not as point estimates but as the range a defensible
analysis can produce.

\subsection*{Every Defensible Specification, at Once}

Four analytic choices in this pipeline have no principled answer---the passage
size, whether to screen genre-diagnostic features and how hard, whether to
weight by inverse density, and whether to variance-match.  Crossing them gives
\SPtotal{} specifications across \SPsizes{} passage sizes, each a complete
leave-one-book-out run with its own jackknife+ intervals.  Reporting one and
relegating the rest to an appendix would invite the reader to treat the
reported figure as privileged, which it is not.  Fig~\ref{fig:speccurve} shows
all of them, ordered by how well each orders the anchors once genre is held
fixed.  \SPpass{} of \SPtotal{} clear the validation threshold of
$\rho_{\text{genre}} > 0.20$.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.98\textwidth]{figures/fig_speccurve.pdf}
\caption{{\bf All \SPtotal{} specifications.}  Point estimates with 68\%
jackknife+ intervals for the three sources under every combination of passage
size, feature screen, weighting and calibration, ordered by genre-controlled
Spearman $\rho$.  Open circles fail validation.  The lower panel marks which
choices are active in each specification.  The intervals never narrow, and no
analytic choice organizes the estimates.}
\label{fig:speccurve}
\end{figure}

Across the \SPpass{} validated specifications, the Deuteronomic source falls
after 586~BCE in \SPDpost{} of \SPpass{} and the Priestly source in
\SPPpost{} of \SPpass---without exception.  The JE composite falls after the
exile in \SPJEpost{} of \SPpass.  Median estimates are \SPJEmed{} BCE for JE,
\SPDmed{} for D and \SPPmed{} for P, with full ranges of \SPJElo--\SPJEhi,
\SPDlo--\SPDhi{} and \SPPlo--\SPPhi{} BCE.  Averaged over validated
specifications, the share of the 68\% interval falling after the exile is
\SPJEmass\% for JE, \SPDmass\% for D and \SPPmass\% for P.

The conclusion the evidence supports is therefore that D and P are
post-exilic, and that JE is very probably so but not securely: three
specifications place it before the exile.  The central estimates fall in the
Persian period.  The Hellenistic era is not excluded---\SPPhell{} of \SPpass{}
specifications place P after 332~BCE---but it is not where the estimates point,
and no validated specification places JE or D that late.

Reading the lower panel of Fig~\ref{fig:speccurve} against the upper ones, no
analytic choice sorts the estimates: the best-validating specifications give
substantially the same answer as the worst.  One choice does affect validation
itself.  Screening out the half of the features that best discriminate genre
raises mean genre-controlled $\rho$ from \SPscreenAll{} to \SPscreenHalf.
Weighting and calibration make no difference to it at all.

Point estimates for every undated unit under a single reference
specification, with their intervals, are given in S8 Table and S1 Fig.  They
are placed there rather than here deliberately: a table of dates invites
exactly the reading this section argues against, and the specification curve
above is the honest summary of what the model supports.

The relative ordering is JE $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ P, the classical
sequence of the documentary hypothesis, recovered from linguistic evidence
alone by a model trained only on independently anchored prophetic and
post-exilic books.  The ordering is better supported than any of the dates.
With intervals of \SPPhalf~yr, the three sources overlap substantially, and the
ordering rests on the model's demonstrated ability to order rather than on
separation between point estimates.

\subsection*{The Archaic Poems and an Extraction Artifact}

The three poems traditionally regarded as the oldest Hebrew
verse~\cite{Albright1968,Cross1975,Robertson1972} needed a correction before
they could be dated at all.

Poems in this corpus are conventionally identified by chapter, but the chapters
containing them also contain prose.  Exodus~15 is \poemSeaProseFrac\% prose by
word count, and Deuteronomy~32 is \poemMosesProseFrac\%.  Because narrative is
systematically placed late by this model, including the prose frame drags the
poem's estimate later.  The effect is not small.  The Song of the Sea moves from
\poemSeaChap{} BCE when extracted as a whole chapter to \poemSea{} BCE when
extracted at verse precision (Exod~15:1--18).  The verse-precise figures are the
ones reported here; the chapter-level ones are an artifact, and the convention
that produces them is widespread.

At verse precision the Song of the Sea is placed at \poemSea{} BCE
(\poemSealo--\poemSeahi, $P(\text{post-exilic}) = \poemSeapost$), and the Song
of Deborah at \poemDeb{} BCE (\poemDeblo--\poemDebhi, \poemDebpost).  These are
the two earliest of the \NTargets{} undated units, agreeing with a century of
philological argument that they are the oldest surviving Hebrew, and arrived at
without any training on them.

The prose continuation of the Song of the Sea (Exod~15:19--27) is placed at
\poemSeaProse{} BCE, \poemSeaGap~yr later than the poem it follows.  A gap of
that size between adjacent verses is itself evidence that the poem is not a
composition of its narrative frame.  Whether such a gap could have been
manufactured is taken up below.

The Song of Moses (Deut~32:1--43) is placed at \poemMoses{} BCE
(\poemMoseslo--\poemMoseshi, \poemMosespost), appreciably later than the other
two and straddling the exile.  A reading of its contents would not predict this.
Its divine-council theology, in which Elyon apportions the nations among the
gods and YHWH receives Israel as his share (32:8--9), is usually taken as among
the most archaic material in the Hebrew Bible.  But the model sees the language rather than the theology, and the language is
late.  Whether the archaic theology of these verses was preserved in a later
idiom, or whether the linguistic estimate is simply wrong for a text this short,
cannot be settled from the present evidence.

\subsection*{Applying the Genre Correction to Everything}

The genre effect established in the Validation section bears on every estimate
in this one, and it must be applied symmetrically or not at all.  A correction
imposed only where it strengthens a conclusion is not a correction.

The clearest single case is Lamentations, whose date is fixed by its subject
matter---it laments the destruction of 586~BCE---making it as securely anchored
as any text in the corpus.  The model places it at \lamPred{} BCE against a
true \lamTruth{} BCE, an error of \lamErr~yr toward greater antiquity.
Lamentations is poetry, and poetry as a class carries a mean residual of
\genPoetry~yr.

For the poems, correcting in the direction the residual indicates makes the
claim weaker, and it survives.  Subtracting the full \genPoetryAbs~yr poetic
residual moves the Song of the Sea from \poemSea{} to \genSeaAdj{} BCE and the
Song of Deborah from \poemDeb{} to \genDebAdj{} BCE.  Both remain pre-exilic,
both remain the earliest of the \NTargets{} undated units, and their
probability of being post-exilic rises only to \genSeaPadj{} and \genDebPadj.
For the Song of the Sea to cross the exile the genre effect would have to be
\genRatio{} times the value observed in Lamentations.

For the sources, the same correction runs the other way, and I report it on the
same terms.  JE is largely narrative, and narrative carries a residual of
\GNoffNar~yr.  Applying it moves JE from \srcJE{} to \GNadjJE{} BCE, D to
\GNadjD{} and P to \GNadjP.  The minimum probability of post-exilic composition
across the three falls from \GNminUncorr{} to \GNminNar.  All three remain
post-exilic, and the ordering is unchanged, but the margin on JE becomes thin.
This is the single largest adjustment any defensible correction makes to the
results above, and it is the reason JE is described throughout as probably
rather than securely post-exilic.

D and P are largely legal material, a register with no anchor at all in this
corpus---the \HBbooks{} anchors contain no law.  Their correction is therefore
bounded rather than known: between \GNoffPro~yr if legal prose behaves like
prophecy and \GNoffNar~yr if it behaves like narrative, giving minimum
post-exilic probabilities of \GNminPro{} and \GNminNar{} respectively.  Both
bounds leave D and P after the exile.  Extending the anchored corpus to include
dated legal material is the obvious way to replace that bound with a
measurement, and I know of no candidate that does not import the circularity
this paper is arguing against.

% =====================================================================
\section*{The Price of Archaizing}
\label{sec:archaizing}
% =====================================================================

Everything above depends on one premise: that the language of a text reflects
when it was written rather than when its author wished to seem to be writing.
The size of the gap between those two things is measured here, first by
performing archaizing on Hebrew directly, and then by turning to Greek texts
whose authors performed it themselves.

\subsection*{Synthetic Archaizing in Hebrew}

Take a securely dated \emph{late} book, replace its \lbh{} forms with their
\cbh{} counterparts at a controlled rate $r$, re-extract all \HBfeat{} features
from the modified text, and re-date it with a model trained on the other 24
books.  Since I performed the substitution myself, the ground
truth is known exactly.

The substitutions are the classical diagnostics of the \cbh{}/\lbh{}
literature, applied in the \lbh{} $\rightarrow$ \cbh{} direction: the relative
particle \textit{še-} $\rightarrow$ \textit{ašer}; the first-person pronoun
\textit{an\={\i}} $\rightarrow$ \textit{ank\={\i}}; \textit{malk\={u}t}
$\rightarrow$ \textit{maml\={a}k\={a}h}; and the negator
\textit{\textquotesingle \={e}n} $\rightarrow$ \textit{l\={o}\textquotesingle},
which changes part of speech as well as lexeme.  Substitution is applied at
the token level before feature extraction, so every downstream feature ---
lexeme rates, part-of-speech transitions, phrase types, clause relations ---
sees the altered text exactly as it would if a scribe had written it that way.
The rate $r$ runs from 0 to 1, and at $r = 1$ not one \lbh{} token of these
types survives anywhere in the book.

\input{tables/tab_archaize}

Total lexical archaizing moves the estimated date by a mean of \arcMean~yr,
with a maximum of \arcMax~yr across the \arcN{} books (Table~\ref{tab:archaize}).
The response is gradual rather than thresholded, as there is no substitution
rate at which the estimate suddenly jumps.

However, three of the six books had almost nothing to substitute, with Ezra
offering \arcEzraTokens{} eligible tokens in the entire book, so their null
results carry little information.  One cannot archaize a text that already lacks the forms.
Among the \arcInfN{} books with substantial substitution density, the exchange
rate is about \arcRate~yr of apparent antiquity per substitution per 1000 words.
Ecclesiastes at $r = 1$ has \arcEccDens{} substitutions per 1000 words, roughly
one word in thirty replaced, which is a density no scribe sustains across a
book, and it moves \arcEccShift~yr.

\subsection*{Where the Model's Leverage Lies}

The reason for so small a number is visible in the model's coefficients.
\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_archaize.pdf}
\caption{{\bf The price of archaizing, by mechanism.}  {\bf A}, Hebrew:
apparent antiquity gained as Late Biblical Hebrew forms are replaced by
Classical counterparts at increasing rates in six securely dated late books.
Solid lines are the books with enough eligible tokens for the result to be
informative.  {\bf B}, Greek: displacement of the Second Sophistic Atticizers
under a model trained only on non-archaizing Greek, with the model's own error
on non-archaizing texts shaded for comparison.  Lexical substitution moves an
estimate by tens of years; reconstructed grammar moves it by hundreds.}
\label{fig:archaize}
\end{figure}

Fig~\ref{fig:leverage} gives the change in estimated date produced by a
one-standard-deviation shift in each feature.  Lexical features carry
\sensLexShare\% of the total leverage, but that share is spread across
\sensLexCount{} features, none of which is worth more than \sensTopLever~yr per
standard deviation.  No single word is a lever.  The rest of the leverage sits
in part-of-speech transition rates, verbal aspect and stem distributions, and
clause-relation profiles, which are high-frequency grammatical habits rather
than choices of vocabulary.

Moreover, these are the features that the passage-level design forces the model
to rely on.  Requiring a feature to be measurable within \HBtarget{} words demotes the rare
diagnostic vocabulary, which is the manipulable part of the language, and
promotes high-frequency morphology, which is not.  The resistance to archaizing documented below is therefore a structural
consequence of the passage-level design rather than an additional assumption:
any model constrained to features estimable in a few hundred words will rest on
the same high-frequency morphology.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.62\textwidth]{figures/fig_leverage.pdf}
\caption{{\bf Where the model's leverage lives.}  Share of total leverage on
the date estimate by feature family, where leverage is the absolute change in
estimated date produced by a one-standard-deviation shift in a feature, summed
within family.  Lexical features carry the largest share but spread it across
\sensLexCount{} weak features; the majority of leverage sits in morphology and
syntax.}
\label{fig:leverage}
\end{figure}

This can be put quantitatively.  Because the model is linear in standardized
features, the smallest coordinated feature shift that displaces an estimate by
$D$ years has length $D/\|\boldsymbol\beta\|$ in standard deviations.  For the
\poemSeaGap~yr gap between the Song of the Sea and its prose frame, that comes
to \sensSD{} standard deviations across \sensDim{} dimensions.  What is required
is not a word swap but a systematic re-profiling of a text's morphology and
syntax, sustained across the whole passage.  As the Greek results below show,
this is achievable by authors trained to achieve it.

\subsection*{Greek Archaizing That Really Happened}

The Hebrew experiment simulates archaizing, and it simulates only the lexical
component of it.  Ancient Greek supplies the real thing, already labeled.
During the Second Sophistic, prose authors of the first three centuries CE
deliberately wrote in imitation of Classical Attic, four to seven centuries
after the fact.  The program was explicit and institutional.  Attic prose
composition was taught in the rhetorical schools, dictionaries of permitted
Attic usage were compiled, and the imitation succeeded well enough that its
practitioners were read as models of style for a millennium.  Their dates of
composition are securely known from external evidence.  This is the labeled set
of archaizing texts that Hebrew cannot provide.

The same pipeline was built on a \GKtexts-text corpus of non-archaizing Greek
prose spanning the Classical and Koine periods, partitioned into \GKchunks{}
passages, with \GKfeat{} features.  The texts were collected from the Perseus
and First1KGreek repositories, where an author's corpus is stored one work per
file, so that the orators, the Lives of Plutarch and the dialogues of Lucian
each occupy dozens of separate files.  Collecting only the complete corpus of
each author matters: an earlier version of this corpus resolved a single work
per author and thereby represented Lysias by one speech and Plutarch by one
Life, which left the Classical end of the scale, the part the model most needs,
severely under-sampled.  Greek lacks a morphological annotation
