comparable to \bhsa{}, so hand-built morphosyntactic rates (optative, infinitive
and participle rates, particle and negation rates, the $\tau\tau$ versus
$\sigma\sigma$ contrast, sentence length) are supplemented by word-form,
character n-gram, and function-word bigram rates, all of them high-frequency by
construction as on the Hebrew side.  Under leave-one-text-out, the Greek model
gives \GKmae~yr against \GKmaebase~yr for the constant predictor, a rank
correlation of $\GKrho$, and \GKpair\% pairwise ordering accuracy.  The
replication is therefore a real one, with the same design recovering a
diachronic signal in an unrelated language.

The \GKatt{} Atticizing texts were excluded from training entirely and then
dated (Table~\ref{tab:greek}).

\input{tables/tab_greek}

The mean displacement is \GKattshift~yr, with \GKattearly{} of the \GKatt{}
texts placed earlier than they were written (Fig~\ref{fig:archaize}B).
\GKattmaxname{} is displaced \GKattmaxearly~yr.  Set against the model's own
\GKmae~yr error on non-archaizing texts, this is a large effect.  Deliberate
and professionally trained archaizing displaces a text by more than a full
error width, and in the worst cases by half a millennium.

The displacement also tracks how programmatic an author's Atticism was, which is
the pattern one would expect if it measures imitation rather than noise.  The
strict Atticists are displaced furthest: Libanius by \GKattmaxearly~yr, Arrian
by \GKaArr, Cassius Dio by \GKaDio, Aelius Aristides by \GKaAris,
Philostratus by \GKaPhil, Dio Chrysostom by \GKaChrys, and Lucian by \GKaLuc.  The authors who wrote a literary Koine
rather than a reconstructed Attic are barely moved at all: Plutarch's
\textit{Lives} by \GKaPlut~yr, Strabo by \GKaStrab, and Dionysius' critical
essays by \GKaDionEss.
A dose-response relation of this kind across authors whose Atticizing intensity
is independently described in the literary histories is difficult to obtain from
a model that is merely noisy.

Two features of the Greek corpus bear on how this number should be read.

First, the effect is if anything \emph{understated}, because the training set is
contaminated.  The corpus manifest classifies Aelian, Appian, Diogenes Laertius,
Plotinus, Porphyry, Iamblichus, and the sophistic novelists as Koine, so all of
them were used as non-archaizing training material.  Yet every one is described
in the literary-historical record as classicizing, and the model placed them
among the largest early displacements in the training set even after being told
they were not archaizing.  A training set containing archaizers teaches the
model that late texts look early, which shrinks the measured displacement of the
declared Atticizers.  Since the classification is a scholarly judgment rather
than a datum, I do not adopt one version of it and defend it.  Instead the
measurement is reported under three definitions of the training set: the
manifest's own labels, a stricter classification that reclassifies the authors
named above, and a date-blind variant that discards register labels entirely and
trains only on texts composed before 50~CE, prior to the Second Sophistic
(S6 Table).

The result holds in sign and grows under the stricter definitions.  The mean
displacement is \GKattshift~yr under the manifest's labels, \GKattshiftB~yr
under the stricter classification, and \GKattshiftC~yr under the date-blind
variant, with \GKattearlyTot{} of \GKattTot{} individual texts across the three
placed earlier than they were written.  The stricter variant is worth a further
remark.  It removes eight texts from training, and yet the model's own
leave-one-text-out error \emph{falls} from \GKmae~yr to \GKmaeB~yr while its
rank correlation rises from $\GKrho$ to $\GKrhoB$.  Perhaps this ought to have
been expected.  Removing the suspected
archaizers from the training set makes the date model better, exactly as one
would expect were they genuinely mislabeled.  Nonetheless, the manifest's own
labels are used as the primary specification throughout, since that variant is
the most conservative and the only one requiring no judgment on my part.

Second, the two Atticizers displaced least, Strabo and Dionysius of
Halicarnassus, are the earliest in the set, writing around the turn of the era
when the Atticizing program was still young.  The displacement grows with the
maturity of the movement, which is what one would expect if it measures
imitation rather than noise.

Additionally, text lengths remain uneven, from \GKattminpass{} passages to
\GKattmaxpass, so a short estimate is correspondingly noisy.  The result is not
driven by the short texts: weighting each text by its passage count gives
\GKattshiftW~yr, and restricting to the \GKattbign{} texts with at least 40
passages gives \GKattshiftBig~yr.

\subsection*{The Greek Measurement Under the Same Genre Control}

Genre is the dominant confound in the Hebrew corpus, and the Greek corpus is
structured in a way that invites the same problem.  Its \GKntexts{} training
texts divide into five genres, and genre is correlated with register: the
ancient Attic baseline is oratory-heavy and contains no narrative at all, while
the Koine material is dominated by history and narrative.  A model that had
learned to recognize oratory would look like a model that had learned to
recognize early Greek.  The Atticizers are spread across genres---six
histories, three philosophical works, two orations, two narratives and one
scientific text---but that spread is not by itself a defense.

The Greek model turns out to be markedly less genre-confounded than the Hebrew
one.  \GKbetween\% of the variance in its predictions lies between genres,
against \GNbetween\% for Hebrew, and rank correlation falls only from
$\GKrhoRaw$ to $\GKrhoGenre$ when genre is held fixed, against $\GNrhoRaw$ to
$\GNrhoPartial$.  With \GKntexts{} texts spanning eight centuries rather than
\HBbooks{} books spanning six, there is enough within-genre chronological range
for the model to use.

The displacement itself is almost untouched.  Scoring each Atticizer against
the mean displacement of non-archaizing texts \emph{in its own genre} rather
than against the corpus as a whole moves the mean from \GKshiftRaw{} to
\GKshiftAdj~yr; the genre correction accounts for 2\% of it.  The decisive
comparison is within genre: Atticizing texts are dated \GKwithinAbs~yr
earlier than non-archaizing texts of the same genre (95\% CI \GKwithinAbsLo{}
to \GKwithinAbsHi~yr earlier, bootstrap $p < 0.001$), and \GKwithinNeg{} of the \GKwithinN{}
genres point the same way.  The single exception is scientific prose, which
contributes one Atticizing text.

The archaizing measurement is therefore not a genre effect in disguise.  This
matters more than a routine robustness check would, because the Hebrew half of
the paper argues that genre confounding is severe enough to halve a reported
correlation; a Greek result that had not been put through the same test would
not deserve to be believed.

\subsection*{What the Two Experiments Establish}

The two experiments do not come out the same way, and the asymmetry is the
substantive finding---though not in the form of a price comparison.

Simulated \emph{lexical} archaizing in Hebrew displaces an estimate by
\arcMeanAbs~yr, which is \DETpct\% of this model's residual scale and thus
indistinguishable from no displacement at all.  Real \emph{morphosyntactic}
archaizing in Greek displaces one by \GKattshiftAbs~yr, an order of magnitude
above that model's noise floor.  One arm returns a measurement and the other
returns a non-detection, so the two cannot be divided to yield an exchange rate.
What can be said is that the detectable case is the grammatical one, and that
this falls where the feature-leverage analysis
said it would.  Swapping out diagnostic vocabulary moves a handful of the
\sensLexCount{} weak lexical features and leaves the other half of the model's
leverage untouched.  The Atticizers did not swap vocabulary.  They reconstructed
a grammar, reviving the optative, restoring the
$\mu\acute{\varepsilon}\nu \ldots \delta\acute{\varepsilon}$ articulation,
writing $\tau\tau$ for $\sigma\sigma$, and matching Classical participial
density.  That is the coordinated multi-dimensional shift which the Hebrew
sensitivity analysis identified as the only route to a displacement of
centuries, and they managed it because an entire educational apparatus existed
to teach them how.

The conclusion is therefore conditional rather than absolute, and it ought to be
stated in that form.  Archaizing can defeat a model of this class; the Greek
case demonstrates it.  Whether the cheaper lexical route can do so is not
answered here, because the instrument used to ask is not sensitive enough to
return an answer either way.  What it
takes is not a scribe who knows the old words, but one trained to write the old
grammar and to sustain it across a whole composition.  For any particular text,
then, the question is whether such training existed in its milieu.

For the Hebrew Bible this becomes a historical question, not a statistical
one, and it is not settled here.  The institutional preconditions do
differ sharply between the two cases.  The Second Sophistic had a documented
curriculum of Attic prose composition, lexica of permitted usage, and a literary
culture that rewarded successful imitation, whereas no comparable program of
Classical Hebrew prose composition is attested for the Second Temple period.
The Qumran evidence adduced by the dialectal school~\cite{Young2008} is the
closest analogue, and it is a good deal thinner.  The sectarian scrolls mix
\cbh{} forms with Aramaisms rather than sustaining a consistent Classical
grammar, which on the evidence here would displace their apparent date by tens
of years rather than hundreds.

This bears directly on the archaic poems.  An archaizing account of the early
placement of the Song of the Sea or the Song of Deborah is not excluded by these
results, but it carries a specific and demanding burden.  It must posit
sustained morphosyntactic imitation, of the kind that took the Second Sophistic
a formal curriculum to achieve, rather than the lexical substitution that the
\cbh{}/\lbh{} literature describes and that is measured above at \arcMeanAbs~yr.
No comparable institution is attested for Second Temple Judaism.  The burden is
therefore a heavy one, and it now has a number attached to it.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Discussion}
% =====================================================================

\subsection*{Limitations}

\textbf{Interval width and what the guarantee covers.}  Jackknife+ intervals are
wide here, averaging \jkwidth~yr at the 68\% level, and their distribution-free
warranty is $1-2\alpha$, so the nominal 90\% level is guaranteed only to 80\%.
Empirical coverage on the anchored corpus is \covsixeight\% and \covninety\%,
comfortably above nominal, but that is an observation about this corpus rather
than a guarantee.  No claim in this paper depends on interval width: every substantive
claim is a side-of-the-exile claim, an ordering claim, or a claim about
dispersion, and none rests on where an endpoint falls.  Point dates are
reported only as medians across specifications and should not be quoted to a
century.

\textbf{Exchangeability, on which the intervals depend.}  The jackknife+
guarantee holds for exchangeable observations.  The unit here is the book, and
these \HBbooks{} books are not obviously exchangeable: \GNnProph{} are
prophetic against \GNnNar{} narrative, every narrative anchor is post-exilic,
and genre displaces an estimate by up to \genNarr~yr.  Under exchangeability the coverage floor is $1-2\alpha$; how far it degrades
when exchangeability fails in this particular way is established neither in the
literature nor here.  Empirical coverage on the anchored corpus is above nominal
(\covsixeight\% and \covninety\%), which is reassuring, but it is an observation about
this corpus and not a guarantee.  A reader who doubts the
exchangeability of prophecy and narrative should treat the intervals as
descriptive.

\textbf{Genre.}  Genre, not chronology, is the dominant axis of variation in
this corpus: \GNbetween\% of the variance in the predictions lies between
genres, and rank correlation with true date falls from $\GNrhoRaw$ to
$\GNrhoPartial$ once genre is held fixed.  A within-genre permutation null
establishes that a chronological signal survives ($p = \GNnullP$), but the
surviving signal is roughly half the raw figure, and every number reported here
should be read against the genre-controlled version rather than the raw one.
With one securely dated poetic book and no dated legal text at all, the genre
correction for two of the three sources is a bound rather than a measurement.
This is the largest single weakness of the design, and enlarging the anchored
corpus in genre rather than in size is what would most improve it.

\textbf{The signal is lexical only.}  Refitting on the \RTBfeat{}
morphosyntactic features with every lexeme removed gives a genre-controlled
$\rho$ of $\RTBgenre$ and a within-prophecy $\rho$ of $\RTBproph$.  Whatever
grammatical change occurred over this period is not detectable at this sample
size, so the results speak to lexical diachrony and to nothing else.  A reader
who takes \cbh{}/\lbh{} to be centrally a grammatical distinction will find no
support for it here, in either direction: absence of detection across
\HBbooks{} books is not absence of the phenomenon.

\textbf{Anchor dates that are partly linguistic.}  Six of the \HBbooks{}
anchors rest on literary rather than external grounds, and two of those
(Jonah, Ecclesiastes) are dated partly by the linguistic profile this model
measures.  Refitting on externally anchored books alone drops genre-controlled
$\rho$ to $\RTDgenre$.  That test is confounded---four of the six dropped
books are late prophetic, so it also strips the late end of the within-genre
range---and the two effects cannot be separated with this corpus.  The
circularity is reduced relative to conventional practice but not eliminated.

\textbf{Corpus asymmetry.}  The anchored corpus is skewed post-exilic, because
that is where external synchronisms are dense.  Inverse-density weighting
mitigates but does not remove the skew, and the pre-exilic end of the scale
rests on \HBnpre{} books.  Still, extending the anchored corpus at the early end would do more for this
model than any change of estimator.

\textbf{The two archaizing measurements bound different things.}  Four
substitution pairs is a small vocabulary of archaizing, so the Hebrew
experiment prices only the lexical mechanism, and prices it at the extreme
setting of total replacement.  The Greek experiment prices real imitation but
only at the intensity Second Sophistic authors actually achieved, in a
language whose annotation is coarser than \bhsa{}, and against a training set
whose register classification is a scholarly judgment rather than a datum
(S6 Table reports the sensitivity to that judgment).  Neither experiment
prices sustained morphosyntactic archaizing \emph{in Hebrew}, which is the
quantity a critic of the Song of the Sea result would most want.  Simulating it
would require a model of what Classical Hebrew grammar an imitator could
reconstruct, and no such model exists.

\textbf{The Greek transfer is an analogy rather than a measurement of Hebrew.}
That Greek imitators achieved a \GKattshiftAbs~yr displacement establishes that the
deep mechanism works in principle and gives its rough scale.  It does not
establish that a Hebrew scribe could have done the same, and the claim that
Second Temple Judaism lacked the institutional apparatus is a historical one,
asserted here rather than demonstrated.

\textbf{One database, one text tradition.}  All Hebrew results depend on the
\bhsa{} annotation of the Masoretic text.  Consonantal variants in the
Qumran and Septuagint traditions are not represented, and the Masoretic
vocalization reflects a much later stage of the language than any composition
date discussed here.  The features used are drawn from the consonantal text
and its morphological parse, but the parse itself is a modern scholarly
product.

\subsection*{The Hebrew Experiment Is a Non-Detection, Not a Measurement}

The Hebrew archaizing result is reported above as a small number, and it is
worth being explicit about what a small number means when the instrument
measuring it is this coarse.

Total lexical archaizing of six securely dated late books moves their estimates
by \arcMeanAbs~yr.  The model's own leave-one-out residuals average
\DETresid~yr, and the 68\% jackknife+ interval on a single undated unit has a
half-width of about \DEThalf~yr.  The observed displacement is therefore
\DETpct\% of the noise against which it would have to be seen.  A shift that
size is not distinguishable from no shift at all.

The correct statement is consequently weaker than ``lexical archaizing is
cheap'', and it is a statement about the instrument rather than about scribes:
\emph{this model cannot detect archaizing of this kind}.  It does not follow
that a Persian-period scribe substituting Classical vocabulary would gain
little; it follows that if he did, this model would not notice.  The two
propositions are easy to conflate and only the second is supported here.

Two features of the design explain the non-detection and bound what it can be
generalized to.  The substitution operates on the recognized \cbh{}/\lbh{}
diagnostic pairs, of which only \LXdiagPresent{} of \LXdiagTotal{} are frequent
enough to enter the feature set at all; the rest---the Persian loanwords and
Aramaisms that carry most of the weight in the philological literature---are too
rare to survive a filter that requires a feature to be measurable within
\HBtarget{} words.  And the model's own signal, though entirely lexical, is
spread thinly across \LXnlex{} common lexemes of which none is worth more than
\sensTopLever~yr per standard deviation.  Substituting a handful of diagnostic
items therefore alters a handful of features out of \LXnlex{} and moves the
estimate very little.  A human philologist reasoning from exactly the rare
markers this model discards is not subject to the same insensitivity, and may
well be harder to deceive than the model is.

The Greek experiment is what carries the argument about archaizing, because
there the imitation is real, its authors are known, and the displacement is
\GKattshiftAbs~yr---an order of magnitude above this model's noise floor, and
\GKwithinAbs~yr when each Atticizer is compared only with texts of its own
genre.

\subsection*{What This Means for the Archaic Poems}

The non-detection bears directly on the results most likely to be cited from
this paper, and it cuts against them.

The Song of the Sea is placed at \poemSea{} BCE and the Song of Deborah at
\poemDeb.  Neither is anywhere near the twelfth- or eleventh-century dates
sometimes proposed for them on prosodic and orthographic
grounds~\cite{Albright1968,Cross1975}; on this evidence they are early
monarchic at best.  That gap is worth stating plainly, because a reader who
takes these results as corroborating a very early date for the Song of the Sea
will have read them backwards.

Set beside that, the poems sit closer to the exile than the point estimates
suggest once two displacements are admitted.  Lamentations, the corpus's only
securely dated poetry, is placed \genPoetryAbs~yr earlier than it was written.
Lamentations is not archaizing: it is genuine poetry of its own date, and the
displacement is what poetic register alone buys.  Applying that correction moves
the Song of the Sea to \DETseaAdj{} BCE, leaving \DETseaAdjMargin~yr between it
and the exile---less than one further correction of the same size.

A deliberately archaizing poem would be expected to exceed that figure rather
than match it, since it would carry intentional archaism on top of the register
effect Lamentations already exhibits.  The displacement required to bring the
Song of the Sea to the exile is \DETseaExileX{} times the Lamentations residual,
and to the end of the exile, where the material of Isaiah 40--55 belongs,
\DETseaDeuteroX{} times.  Neither multiple is extravagant for a text composed in
conscious imitation of older verse.

I do not argue that case here; the evidence assembled in this paper cannot
settle it, and the poems' pre-exilic placement remains this study's best
estimate.  What the paper can establish is the shape of the argument that would
be needed.  An exilic Song of the Sea is not excluded by these results---it
requires a register-plus-archaizing displacement of roughly twice what an
unremarkable poetic book already shows, in a model demonstrably unable to detect
archaizing at all.  Whether the poem's language, imagery and theology support
that reading is a question for philology rather than for this model, and one I
intend to take up separately.

\subsection*{Which Analyses Were Planned, and Which Were Not}

This study grew by responding to its own failures, and a reader is entitled to
know which results were sought and which were stumbled into, because the two
carry different evidential weight.

Planned before any result was seen: the corpus and its anchoring, the
passage-level design, the leave-one-book-out protocol, the free-shuffle
permutation null, the archaizing simulation, and the Greek replication.  Those
are confirmatory.

Everything else in this article was prompted by something that had already gone
wrong.  The genre analysis began when narrative books were noticed to be
systematically misplaced; the within-genre null, the feature screen and the
genre-controlled statistic all follow from it.  The lexical-versus-morphosyntactic
ablation was a response to the suspicion that the model was classifying subject
matter.  The specification curve was built after the point estimates proved
unstable.  The block-separation analysis was undertaken as a positive result and
is reported as a negative one.  The feature-encoding comparison came last of
all.  These are exploratory, and the two nulls are the only inferential
statements among them that were computed against a pre-declared number of draws.

The distinction matters most for the block separations, where an exploratory
analysis produced three significant results in the expected direction that a
subsequent control dissolved.  Had the control not been applied, three false
claims would have entered the literature with $p$-values attached.  I report the
sequence rather than the tidied outcome so that the reader can weigh the
exploratory results accordingly.

\subsection*{Scholarly Context for a Late Torah}

The finding that the Pentateuchal sources are post-exilic is not novel in
biblical scholarship, however contested it remains.  A substantial tradition
places the final composition of P in the Persian
period~\cite{Blenkinsopp1996,Nihan2007}, and the ``Persian period
Pentateuch'' position associated with the Copenhagen and Sheffield schools
places the whole compositional process
there~\cite{Davies1992,Lemche1993}.  Against this, Hurvitz's linguistic
argument for a pre-exilic P~\cite{Hurvitz1982,Hurvitz2014} and the broader
neo-documentary position maintain earlier dates.

What is offered here is not the direction of the result but its arrival with a
calibrated uncertainty, an explicit genre control, and a stated limit on what
can be said about archaizing.  The linguistic argument for a pre-exilic P has
always had to assume that the post-exilic appearance of a text cannot be
manufactured, while the argument for a post-exilic P has assumed the converse.
This study constrains the second assumption and, in Greek, the first; in Hebrew
it establishes only that the question is beyond the resolution of a model of
this kind, which is itself worth knowing before the assumption is made again.

\subsection*{Feature Encoding, and a Better Way to Build the Features}

Two questions about the feature encoding were raised late in this work and are
reported because one of them points somewhere useful.

The features are rates per \HBtarget{} words rather than proportions, so a
linear model in them does not imply an impossible value.  But if the trajectory
of a form over time is logistic, as language change generally is, then a model
linear in the raw rate is fitting a curve with a straight line.  Refitting on
transformed rates confirms the mismatch is real but small: $\log(1+x)$ improves
mean absolute error from \FSrawMae{} to \FSlogMae~yr and rank correlation from
$\FSrawRho$ to $\FSlogRho$.  It does nothing for the confound that actually
limits this study---genre-controlled $\rho$ is $\FSlogGenre$ against
$\GNrhoPartial$ unscreened---so the reported model is left on the raw scale.

The second question is more consequential.  A rate per \HBtarget{} words
measures how often an author reaches for a form at all, which is substantially a
matter of genre, mixed together with which of the competing forms he chooses
when he does, which is the diachronic signal.  Variationist linguistics
separates them by dividing within the set of alternants: the share of
\emph{'an\=ok\^\i}{} among first-person singular pronouns, rather than
\emph{'an\=ok\^\i}{} per \HBtarget{} words.  Encoded as a share, that single
variable's genre-controlled correlation with date rises from \FSanokiGenre{} to
\FSshareGenre.

Applied at the scale the corpus currently permits, the effect is larger than one
variable would suggest.  \VTpairs{} alternant pairs have both members above the
frequency filter, of which \VTstrict{} are strict linguistic variables and the
rest near-synonyms an automatic procedure cannot distinguish.  A model built on
those \VTshareFeat{} share features alone---against \HBfeat{} rate
features---gives a genre-controlled $\rho$ of $\VTshareGenre$, well above the
$\GNrhoPartial$ of the full rate model, though its raw correlation
($\VTshareRho$) and error (\VTshareMae~yr) are worse.  That is what the theory
predicts: shares discard the frequency information that genre drives, keeping
only the choice between forms.  Jackknifing over books, the share model's
genre-controlled $\rho$ runs \VTjkLo{} to \VTjkHi{} with a median of
\VTjkMed, against \VTjkRateMed{} for the rate model, and beats it in
\VTjkWin{} of \VTjkN{} single-book deletions.  Combining both feature sets gives
$\VTbothGenre$ at \VTbothMae~yr.

Two controls establish that this is the encoding rather than an artifact of
fitting seven features instead of \HBfeat.  Refitting on the \emph{same fourteen
lexemes} as plain rates---identical linguistic material, differently
encoded---gives a genre-controlled $\rho$ of $\VTctlSame$, less than half the
share encoding's $\VTshareGenre$.  And seven rate features drawn at random give
a median of $\VTctlRandMed$ over \VTctlRandN{} draws, reaching at most
$\VTctlRandMax$; none attains the share model's value.  Parsimony does not
produce this, and neither does the choice of lexemes, since the same-material
control holds those fixed.

The pair list, however, will not bear the weight the comparison invites, and
the reason is worth reporting because it is the same failure the paper documents
elsewhere.  Only \VTlitPairs{} of the \VTpairs{} surviving pairs come from the
diachronic literature---the first-person pronoun~\cite{Rooker1990,Polzin1976}
and the \emph{'el}/\emph{le} merger~\cite{Polzin1976}.  The remaining five were
assembled by me as plausible alternations, and three of them are
not linguistic variables at all but near-synonyms.  Fitted on the two
literature-derived pairs alone the model gives $\VTlitGenre$; on the five
investigator-added pairs it gives $\VTnonlitGenre$.  The result does not come
from the pairs the literature vouches for.

Nor is it stable across the pair set.  Dropping one pair at a time moves
genre-controlled $\rho$ between $\VTlooLo$ and $\VTlooHi$, and the seven-pair
model is one of \VTsubsets{} non-empty subsets that could have been reported.
The number quoted above is therefore a point in a space that was searched after
the outcome was visible, and the specification-curve discipline applied to the
dating results has not been applied to it.

What survives is narrower and worth keeping separate from what does not.  The
\emph{encoding} effect is controlled: identical lexemes, differently encoded,
differ by more than a factor of two, and no random seven-feature model
approaches the share model.  The particular seven-pair \emph{feature set} is
not a result, and I do not offer it as one.  A model built on shares would need
its pair list specified in advance on linguistic grounds, and its own passage
through the specification curve, the permutation nulls and the ablations---which is a study, not a revision.  The reason to say so plainly is that this
encoding is the only change tried here that moved the confound rather than the
accuracy, and that makes it exactly the kind of promising result that a
post-hoc feature list would be most likely to overstate.

\subsection*{Extensibility}

Given a morphologically annotated corpus and a set of externally anchored dates,
the pipeline is indifferent to the language.  The Greek replication was
implemented from the same code with a different feature extractor.  The binding
constraint is annotation rather than method.  Ugaritic, Phoenician, and
epigraphic Hebrew would supply badly needed early anchors, but they lack
comparable morphological parsing.  Producing such a parse for the Iron Age
epigraphic corpus would be the single most valuable contribution to this line of
work.

\subsection*{Relation to Authorship Attribution}

Attribution and dating are complementary.  A method that assigns a text to a
scribal school and a method that assigns it a date constrain different axes of
the same question, and their errors are not the same errors.  One natural
extension would be to use attribution output as a register covariate in the date
model, which would let the genre confound documented above be modeled rather
than merely reported.

% =====================================================================
\section*{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================

Biblical Hebrew carries a diachronic signal strong enough to order books in
time and to separate pre-exilic from post-exilic composition, and far too weak
to date any single text to a century.  Across \SPpass{} defensible
specifications the Deuteronomic and Priestly sources fall after the exile
without exception and the JE composite in \SPJEpost, in the classical sequence
JE $\rightarrow$ D $\rightarrow$ P, with central estimates in the Persian
period.  The Song of the Sea and the Song of Deborah remain the earliest of the
\NTargets{} undated units.  No individual date in this study should be quoted
to a century, and the intervals say so.

Two findings about method matter more than the dates, and both cut against
current practice.  Genre, not chronology, is the dominant axis of variation in a
corpus assembled this way; a study reporting raw rank correlation without
controlling for it overstates its signal by roughly half.  And the diachronic
signal that survives is entirely lexical: refitting on verb morphology, clause
structure and agreement gives nothing.  That is a quantitative datum in a debate
conducted largely by example, and it favors the lexical emphasis of Hurvitz's
method over accounts appealing to grammatical change.

The paper also reports a claim it could not sustain, and I think that is the
most instructive part of it.  Splitting each source at the division its critical
literature already draws produces three significant separations, all in the
expected direction, from a model that was told nothing about those divisions.
Under the genre control the separations disappear and the Deuteronomic one
reverses.  Legal prose and hortatory narrative differ in vocabulary, and that
difference was doing the work.  The unscreened result is precisely what a study
would publish if it stopped one step short of its own control, and it would have
been wrong.  Detecting compositional strata by linguistic date remains a
reasonable ambition; \HBbooks{} anchor books spanning a single religious
literature are not enough to do it, and any future attempt will have to clear
the same bar.

The premise on which all such conclusions rest, that a late author cannot
convincingly write early, has been treated as an assumption for two decades.  It
is measurable, and measuring it shows that it is not one assumption but two,
with different answers.  Complete lexical archaizing of a securely dated late
Hebrew book buys a mean of \arcMeanAbs~yr of apparent antiquity, since the
diagnostic vocabulary that the \cbh{}/\lbh{} literature treats as the substance
of archaizing turns out to carry very little of a passage-level model's
leverage.  The Second Sophistic Atticizers, who reconstructed Classical grammar
rather than Classical vocabulary and were trained by a formal curriculum to do
so, are pushed \GKattshiftAbs~yr too early.

Archaizing therefore has a price, and that price is set by how deep the
imitation reaches.  This is a more useful result than immunity would have been,
as it converts a rhetorical impasse into a comparison that can be made case by
case.  For any text whose date is disputed on linguistic grounds, the question is
no longer whether archaizing is possible in the abstract, but whether the milieu
in question supported the deep kind of it.  For the Second Sophistic the answer
is documented and affirmative.  For Second Temple Judaism no comparable program
is attested, and the closest analogue, the Qumran sectarian scrolls that mix
Classical forms with Aramaisms rather than sustaining a Classical grammar,
resembles the cheap mechanism rather than the expensive one.

\section*{Data Availability}
% =====================================================================

All code, extracted feature matrices, model outputs, and the scripts that
regenerate every table, figure and numerical claim in this article are
available at \url{https://github.com/adairaar/diachronic-hebrew}.  The
repository includes \texttt{run\_pipeline.py}, which executes the analysis end
to end and verifies its own output (see \emph{Computational reproducibility}
below).

Two inputs are third-party and are not redistributed.  The \bhsa{} database is
available under its own license from the Eep Talstra Centre for Bible and
Computer and is retrieved automatically by the Text-Fabric access layer on
first run; the repository records the version used.  Greek texts derive from
the open First1KGreek and Perseus collections and are retrieved by a script in
the repository.  No other data are required.
